notYet: Not yet part of the Eastern Mediterranean

stages.name: Loyal to Persia
stages.desc: Obeys the Great King and his satraps

stages.name: Independent Egypt
stages.desc: Ruled by native pharaohs, free of Persia since 404 BC

stages.name: Reconquered & punished
stages.desc: Retaken by force, or surrendered to the king's armies

states.name: Cyprus
timeline: Cyprus's city-kings rule as subjects of Persia; Pumiyaton takes the throne of Phoenician Kition about now
Following the Phoenicians' example, the kings of Cyprus's nine cities rise together against Persia
Idrieus of Caria lands forty triremes and eight thousand mercenaries for Persia and besieges Salamis
The cities submit one by one; Pnytagoras of Salamis, the last to yield, keeps his throne

states.name: Israel
timeline: The coast south of Phoenicia stays in Persian hands; Acre had been Persia's base against Egypt
Tachos's Egyptian army and its Greek mercenaries come up the coast road
Later Christian writers claim Persian reprisals in Judea and deportations, an account historians dispute

states.name: Palestine
timeline: Gaza guards the coast road between Persia's Syria and free Egypt
Persian armies pass through on their way to the failed invasion of Egypt
Later writers claim Jericho was punished and its people deported, a disputed tradition
The Great King's army takes the coast road through Gaza toward Egypt

states.name: Lebanon
timeline: Diodorus lists the Phoenicians among the coastal peoples who rise against the king
Pharaoh Tachos marches into Phoenicia; Sidon's king Straton seems to keep defying Persia
On one reading of its coins, Sidon is crushed and occupied for about four years, its currency banned
Under King Tennes, Sidon cuts down the royal park, burns the cavalry's fodder and seizes Persian officials
Tennes betrays Sidon and the city burns; the other Phoenician cities submit in terror
Coins struck at Sidon now carry the name of the Persian satrap Mazaeus

states.name: Syria
timeline: Diodorus names the Syrians among the rebels of the coast
The revolt collapses and Egypt's invasion of Phoenicia falls apart; the satrapy returns to the king
The satrap Belesys holds Syria for Persia, though the island city of Arados sits on Phoenicia's common council
The Great King's army gathers on the road south to Sidon

states.name: Turkey
timeline: The heart of the Satraps' Revolt: Ariobarzanes, Mausolus, Orontes, Autophradates and the Cilicians defy the king
Betrayals and assassinations break the revolt; the western satraps make their peace
Artabazus rebels in Hellespontine Phrygia with Athenian help, a local rising that is over within a few years
Mazaeus of Cilicia marches against the Phoenician rebels for Persia
Idrieus of Caria supplies the fleet and mercenaries sent against Cyprus

states.name: Jordan
timeline: The Transjordan lands stay quiet under Persian rule, outside the fighting
Beaten by his own nephew, Pharaoh Tachos flees across Arabia to the Persian king

states.name: Egypt
timeline: Free of Persia since 404 BC, and now paying Greek mercenaries to carry the war into Asia
Nectanebo II overthrows Tachos while the army is in Phoenicia
Artaxerxes III's first invasion fails, and Nectanebo sends mercenaries to help Sidon
Pelusium, Bubastis and Memphis fall; Nectanebo flees south and Egypt's temples are plundered

states.name: N. Cyprus
timeline: Cyprus's city-kings rule as subjects of Persia; Pumiyaton takes the throne of Phoenician Kition about now
Following the Phoenicians' example, the kings of Cyprus's nine cities rise together against Persia
Idrieus of Caria lands forty triremes and eight thousand mercenaries for Persia and besieges Salamis
The cities submit one by one; Pnytagoras of Salamis, the last to yield, keeps his throne

states.name: Cyprus U.N. Buffer Zone
timeline: Cyprus's city-kings rule as subjects of Persia; Pumiyaton takes the throne of Phoenician Kition about now

events.title: Satraps' Revolt
events.text: Diodorus says satraps and coastal peoples from Lydia to Phoenicia rose together, cutting off half the king's revenue.

events.title: Orontes changes sides
events.text: Chosen as the rebels' general, Orontes keeps a year's pay for 20,000 mercenaries and hands cities over to the king.

events.title: Arrests at Leucae
events.text: Rheomithres takes 500 talents and fifty warships from Egypt, then sends the rebel leaders to the king in irons.

events.title: Ariobarzanes betrayed
events.text: The satrap of Phrygia is handed over by his own son Mithridates and executed.

events.title: Datames assassinated
events.text: The formidable satrap of Cappadocia survives open battle, only to be killed in a plot the king arranged.

events.title: Pumiyaton of Kition
events.text: A Phoenician dynasty on Cyprus passes to a new king, who will rule the city for half a century.

events.title: Tachos arms Egypt
events.text: The pharaoh gathers 200 triremes, 10,000 Greek mercenaries and 80,000 Egyptian troops to strike at Persia.

events.title: Agesilaus arrives
events.text: Sparta's aged king reaches Egypt to command Tachos's mercenaries, while the Athenian Chabrias takes the fleet.

events.title: Tachos invades Phoenicia
events.text: Egypt's army and its Greek mercenaries march up the coast and carry the war into Persian Asia.

events.title: Nectanebo seizes power
events.text: With the army abroad, Tachos's nephew wins over the troops and takes the throne as Nectanebo II.

events.title: Tachos flees
events.text: The fallen pharaoh escapes by way of Arabia to the Persian king, who pardons him.

events.title: Ochus becomes king
events.text: Artaxerxes III comes to the throne in the winter of 359–358 BC and, Justin says, kills his own relatives to keep it.

events.title: Straton defies Persia
events.text: On one modern reading of Sidon's coins, its king, honoured by Athens as a friend, is at war with Persia's generals.

events.title: Artabazus rebels
events.text: A satrap in northwest Anatolia rises against the new king and hires the Athenian general Chares.

events.title: The king's threat
events.text: Athens makes peace with its rebel allies and recalls Chares, on word that the king will send 300 ships against it.

events.title: Sidon occupied
events.text: On the same reading of the coins, Persia crushes Sidon and bans its currency for about four years.

events.title: Mausolus dies
events.text: Caria's dynast, once listed among the rebels, dies at Halicarnassus, leaving the tomb that gives us the word mausoleum.

events.title: Ochus fails in Egypt
events.text: The king's first great invasion ends in defeat, and the Egyptians, Diodorus says, come to despise him.

events.title: Tennes takes the throne
events.text: Coins suggest that Tennes, in Phoenician Tabnit, now rules Sidon.

events.title: Council at Tripolis
events.text: Arados, Sidon and Tyre share this city, where the Phoenicians hold their common council; Sidon, mistreated by Persian officials, resolves to revolt.

events.title: The royal park felled
events.text: Sidon's first act of war is to cut down the Persian kings' park, burn the cavalry's fodder and seize Persians.

events.title: Mentor reaches Sidon
events.text: Nectanebo sends Tennes 4,000 Greek mercenaries under Mentor of Rhodes.

events.title: Satraps defeated
events.text: Tennes and Mentor beat Belesys of Syria and Mazaeus of Cilicia and drive the Persians out of Phoenicia.

events.title: Cyprus rises
events.text: Nine Cypriot cities, each with its own king, follow Phoenicia and declare themselves independent.

events.title: Athens says no
events.text: Asked for troops, Athens and Sparta decline; Thebes sends 1,000 hoplites and Argos 3,000.

events.title: The king marches
events.text: Ochus leads the army from Babylon himself; Diodorus gives 300,000 infantry and 30,000 cavalry, numbers no one can verify.

events.title: Phocion besieges Salamis
events.text: Sent by Idrieus of Caria, the Athenian Phocion and Evagoras, a pretender to the throne, attack Cyprus's greatest city.

events.title: The secret offer
events.text: Tennes's agent Thettalion reaches the king with an offer to betray Sidon and guide him into Egypt.

events.title: The hundred shot down
events.text: Tennes leads Sidon's hundred leading citizens out of the walls and into the king's hands, and they are shot down.

events.title: Olive branches
events.text: Five hundred more Sidonians come out as suppliants begging mercy, and are killed still holding their branches.

events.title: Sidon burns
events.text: With the city taken, families burn themselves in their homes; Diodorus counts more than 40,000 dead.

events.title: Tennes executed
events.text: His usefulness over, the man who betrayed Sidon is put to death by the king he served.

events.title: The ashes sold
events.text: The king sells the ruins for many talents, for the gold and silver the fire had melted.

events.title: Prisoners reach Babylon
events.text: A Babylonian chronicle records Sidonian captives arriving in the autumn, and women taken into the king's palace.

events.title: Reprisals in Judea?
events.text: Later Christian writers claim Jericho suffered and Jews were deported to Hyrcania, a tradition historians dispute.

events.title: Salamis yields
events.text: The last rebel city on Cyprus submits, and King Pnytagoras is allowed to keep his throne.

events.title: Mazaeus at Sidon
events.text: The satrap Tennes once defeated now strikes coins at Sidon under his own name.

events.title: The Barathra marshes
events.text: Marching on Egypt, the Persian army loses men in the treacherous marshes east of the Nile delta.

events.title: Pelusium surrenders
events.text: After Greek fought Greek, the garrison of Egypt's eastern gate gives up on a promise of safe passage.

events.title: Bubastis opens
events.text: Mentor spreads word that cities that yield will be spared, and Egyptians and Greeks turn on each other.

events.title: Nectanebo flees
events.text: The last native pharaoh abandons Memphis and escapes south toward Nubia.

events.title: Temples plundered
events.text: Ochus loots Egypt's sanctuaries and their sacred records, and installs Pherendates as satrap.

chartNote: Share of the area of today's countries, a simplification: the regions are modern boundaries, each given one colour, though Anatolia, Syria and Phoenicia were divided among loyalists and rebels. Dates are approximate. Diodorus places these wars in 351–349 BC, while the modern chronology followed here dates the fall of Sidon to about 345 and the conquest of Egypt to 343, and some scholars prefer 340/339. Sidon's revolt and occupation of about 360–351 is a modern inference from its coins. Egypt's vast area dominates the shares.
